title: The past tense of regular verbs
why: First lesson of level A2: after the four-form present, you discover the past tense, which is conjugated with person endings. It's the foundation of any story: your day, your weekend, a trip.

{"lessons": ["

One past tense, with endings

Good news: Hebrew has only one past tense. Where English chooses between \"I wrote,\" \"I have written,\" \"I was writing,\" and \"I used to write,\" Hebrew always says כָּתַבְתִּי [katavti].

In the present, the verb only changed for gender and number (כּוֹתֵב, כּוֹתֶבֶת, כּוֹתְבִים, כּוֹתְבוֹת). In the past, it changes for person (I, you, he, we…): you add an ending to the base כָּתַב [katav], \"he wrote.\" English verbs don't do this, but the system is very regular.

כָּתַבhe wrote: the base, with no ending [katav]
כָּתַבְתִּיI wrote: the base + ti [katavti]

The past base, כָּתַב, is the \"he\" form: it's also the form you find in dictionaries. Its three consonants כ ת ב make up the root, which you also find in כּוֹתֵב and לִכְתֹּב.

", "

The full table

PronounPastPronunciationEnding

אַתָּהכָּתַבְתָּkatavta־תָּ (ta)
אַתְּכָּתַבְתְּkatavt־תְּ (t)
הוּאכָּתַבkatavnone
הִיאכָּתְבָהkatvaa (final ה)
אֲנַחְנוּכָּתַבְנוּkatavnu־נוּ (nu)
אַתֶּםכְּתַבְתֶּםktavtem־תֶּם (tem)
אַתֶּןכְּתַבְתֶּןktavten־תֶּן (ten)
הֵם / הֵןכָּתְבוּkatvuוּ (u)

Three things to notice:

  • I and we don't change for gender: a woman and a man both say כָּתַבְתִּי. In the present, it was כּוֹתֵב / כּוֹתֶבֶת.
  • You, however, does change: כָּתַבְתָּ [katavta] to a man, כָּתַבְתְּ [katavt] to a woman.
  • They (m.) and they (f.) share the same form: הֵם כָּתְבוּ, הֵן כָּתְבוּ. With הִיא and הֵם, the second vowel drops out: כָּתְבָה [katva], כָּתְבוּ [katvu].

For אַתֶּם, you'll often hear [katavtem] on the street; [ktavtem] is the correct form, the one used in books and on the radio.

", "

The pronoun: optional or required?

The ending already tells you who did the action: unlike English, but as in Spanish or Italian, the pronoun is optional in the 1st and 2nd person.

לָמַדְתִּי עִבְרִית בָּאוּלְפָּן.I studied Hebrew at the ulpan. [lamadti ivrit ba-ulpan]
כְּבָר אָכַלְתָּ?Have you eaten yet? (to a man) [kvar akhalta?]

In the 3rd person, no ending says \"he\" or \"they\": keep the pronoun or the subject.

הוּא עָבַד כָּל הַיּוֹם.He worked all day. [hu avad kol ha-yom]
נֹעָה וְרוֹן רָקְדוּ כָּל הַלַּיְלָה.Noa and Ron danced all night. [No'a ve-Ron rakdu kol ha-laila]

Negation doesn't change: לֹא before the verb. עוֹד לֹא גָּמַרְתִּי. I haven't finished yet. [od lo gamarti]

With אָכַל and עָבַד, which begin with א or ע, the shva of \"you\" (plural) becomes a short a: אֲכַלְתֶּם [akhaltem], עֲבַדְתֶּם [avadtem]. Everything else follows the table of כָּתַב.
